source.version: EPDE 2024 conference paper, EPDE2024/1149 (5–6 September 2024); complete six-page PDF on file, including references.
source.title_on_document: HOW CAN AI SUPPORT THE CREATION OF NOVEL IDEAS IN PRODUCT DESIGN

paper_design_summary: Postgraduate students in a Design Methods class generated kitchen-product ideas for people with arthritis through group brainwriting, with permission to use ChatGPT, Google, or neither. The paper specifies which groups received each condition but does not state how groups or conditions were allocated. Coders assessed the novelty of the resulting concepts and reported team averages; a separate survey assessed participants’ experiences.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Groups were permitted to use ChatGPT, Google, or neither during brainwriting; the mechanism for forming groups or assigning conditions is not stated. This is a classroom comparison with an unstated allocation mechanism, so an RCT or explicitly nonrandom design cannot be established.
assignment.quote: The class was then divided into five groups. Due to class numbers, we had three groups of six students and two groups of five students.
assignment.locator: PDF pp. 2–3, section 2.1, Design & Delivery of the experiment (group formation on p. 2 and allocation of support across pp. 2–3).

arms.name: ChatGPT support
arms.description: Two groups of six students were permitted to use ChatGPT after exhausting their own ideas; section 2.1 reports 12 survey responses received. These are group-membership and survey-response counts, not a separately stated analyzed count for novelty (PDF p. 2, section 2.1).

arms.name: Google support
arms.description: One group of six students was permitted to use Google after exhausting their own ideas; section 2.1 reports 5 survey responses received. A separate analyzed participant count for novelty is not stated (PDF pp. 2–3, section 2.1).

arms.name: No additional support (control)
arms.description: Two groups of five students were not permitted to use ChatGPT or Google and undertook traditional 5-3-5 brainwriting; section 2.1 reports 9 survey responses received. A separate analyzed participant count for novelty is not stated (PDF p. 3, continuation of section 2.1).

participants.exclusions: Survey only: one participant in the traditional group did not respond; one Google respondent and one ChatGPT respondent were excluded because they were thought to have misunderstood the questions. The paper states that 25 survey responses remained for analysis (PDF p. 3, section 3.1, first paragraph). For the subsequent helpfulness analysis, one Google respondent and three ChatGPT respondents reported never running out of ideas and therefore not using the tools; their results were removed, leaving the stated 12 respondents (PDF p. 3, section 3.1, second paragraph; PDF p. 4, continuation of section 3.1). The paper does not state that these exclusions applied to concept-novelty coding (PDF p. 3, section 2.2; PDF p. 4, section 3.2 and Table 2).
participants.who: Postgraduate students at the University of Strathclyde taking a Design Methods module, with mixed prior design experience. The paper states that 28 students were asked to participate (PDF p. 2, section 2.1). The stated 25 analyzed responses belong only to the feedback survey after nonresponse and exclusions (PDF p. 3, section 3.1). The number of people whose concepts contributed to the novelty analysis is not separately stated, so n_analyzed is null. Arm descriptions retain the response counts printed in section 2.1 rather than treating them as analyzed novelty counts.
participants.quote: Based on this, we had twenty-five responses for our analysis.
participants.locator: PDF p. 2, section 2.1 (cohort and population); PDF p. 3, section 3.1, Survey Feedback (quoted analyzed survey count); PDF p. 4, section 3.2 and Table 2 (novelty results by team without a separate people count).

ai_tool.how_used: Students in the ChatGPT condition could consult it only once they felt they had exhausted their own ideas, to support further idea generation during brainwriting. Google web searching was a separate comparator (PDF pp. 2–3, section 2.1).

task.description: Act as product-design consultants and generate concepts for a new product that makes kitchen tasks easier for an arthritis sufferer. Groups of six used 6-3-5 brainwriting and groups of five used 5-3-5; participants first listed and discussed kitchen challenges (PDF p. 2, section 2.1).
task.duration: Total session duration not stated. The paper describes the 6-3-5 method as involving a 5-minute timeframe (PDF p. 1, section 1).

outcomes.name: Concept novelty (intercoder ratings averaged by team)
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: Table 2 reports Group Average scores: ChatGPT group 1, -2.33; ChatGPT group 2, -3.89; control group 4, -5.06; control group 5, -4.33. The Google group 3 score is -2.89. Scores closer to 0 indicate higher novelty. No pooled ChatGPT-versus-control estimate, standard deviation, standard error, confidence interval, or inferential test is reported.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4, section 3.2, Intercoder Analysis, and Table 2, Results of Intercoder Analysis; PDF p. 3, section 2.2 (concept coding and averaging by team).

eligibility.reason: The paper reports division of a class into groups and permission to use ChatGPT, Google, or neither, but does not state random assignment or another allocation mechanism (PDF pp. 2–3, section 2.1); criterion 1 therefore remains unclear. Only 28 students were asked to participate (PDF p. 2, section 2.1), and 25 survey responses were analyzed (PDF p. 3, section 3.1), so the study cannot meet the 50-person threshold even though the novelty-analysis participant count is not separately stated. Concepts were scored for novelty by coders and averaged by team (PDF p. 3, section 2.2; PDF p. 4, section 3.2 and Table 2), satisfying criterion 3. Core is no because of sample size; observational context is not established because a nonrandom allocation mechanism is not stated.

one_line_finding: ChatGPT groups had novelty scores of -2.33 and -3.89 versus -5.06 and -4.33 for controls, with scores closer to zero indicating greater novelty, in a classroom comparison whose allocation method is unstated (PDF p. 4, section 3.2 and Table 2; allocation description on pp. 2–3, section 2.1).
